                    ### Question
                    Question linked to image nº16 A 54-year-old black woman with asthenia, drowsiness, paresthesias, gait disorder, and loss of strength and sensation in both lower extremities. The analyzes showed Hb 10.4 g / dL, VCM 107 fL, platelets 110,000 / mm3, leukocytes 5,000 / mm3, neutrophils 1900 / mm3, lymphocytes 2500 / mm3, monocytes 300 / mm3, eosinophils 300 / mm3, reticulocytes 1.0% (normal: 0.5-2), total reticulocytes 5,400 / mm3, haptoglobin 0 g / L (normal 0.3-2 g / L), LDH 1,114 U / L, AST (GOT) 50 U / L, ALT ( GPT) 30 U / L, GGT 16 U / L, alkaline phosphatase 90 U / L, total bilirubin 1.03 mg / dL. Negative Coombs test. The peripheral blood smear is shown in the image. Assessed the clinical and analytical picture, what is the treatment that should be administered to this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Plasmatic exchange.
opb. Oral corticosteroids
opc. Parenteral vitamin B12.
opd. Folic acid and splenectomy.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 54-year-old black woman, including macrocytic anemia (Hb 10.4 g/dL, VCM 107 fL), neurological symptoms (asthenia, paresthesias, gait disorder), and laboratory findings (negative Coombs test, low haptoglobin, high LDH), strongly suggest vitamin B12 deficiency. The negative Coombs test rules out autoimmune hemolytic anemia, while the low reticulocyte count indicates inadequate erythropoiesis. Given these factors, parenteral vitamin B12 is the most appropriate treatment, as it directly addresses the underlying deficiency causing the macrocytic anemia and associated neurological symptoms. Evidence supporting this includes the established role of vitamin B12 in preventing megaloblastic anemia and its neurological manifestations. Other options, such as oral corticosteroids, folic acid, and splenectomy, do not align with the clinical picture and are not indicated in this case.
